essence: Laudomia is triple: beside the living city lie the city of its dead, which explains it with reassuring order, and the city of the unborn, which answers only with alarm; together the dead and the unborn are the two bulbs of an hourglass never turned over, each life a grain passing through the living city at the neck.
textDetails: Like every city, Laudomia has a second city beside it whose inhabitants carry the same names: the Laudomia of the dead, its cemetery.
Its peculiarity is that it is triple: there is a third Laudomia, the city of the unborn.
The more the living city grows and crowds, the more the field of tombs outside the walls expands.
The streets of the city of the dead are barely wide enough for the gravedigger's cart, and many windowless buildings line them.
Its street plan and the layout of its dwellings repeat those of the living city, and in both, families are squeezed ever tighter into compartments stacked one above another.
On fine afternoons the living go to visit the dead and make out their own names on the stone slabs.
The city of the dead recounts the same history of toil, anger, illusions and feelings, except that there everything has become necessary, removed from chance, filed and set in order.

To be sure of itself the living city looks for its explanation among the dead, risking finding more or less than it wants: explanations for more than one Laudomia, for cities that could have been and were not, or reasons that are partial, contradictory, disappointing.
The unborn are given an equally vast dwelling, though not in proportion to their presumably infinite number; it stands empty, enclosed by architecture made of niches, bays and grooves.

Since the unborn can be pictured at any size, as small as mice, silkworms, ants or ants' eggs, one can imagine them standing or crouching on every bracket, capital and plinth that projects from the walls, lined up or dispersed, absorbed in the business of their future lives.

In a vein of the marble one can glimpse Laudomia a hundred or a thousand years from now, crowded with people in never-seen clothing, all in eggplant-coloured barracans, for instance, or with turkey feathers in their turbans, pursuing affairs, revenges, marriages for love or for money.

The living come to the house of the unborn and question them silently while their steps resound under the empty domes; they ask only about themselves, one wanting an illustrious memory, another wanting his shame forgotten, but the harder they look the less they can trace a continuous thread; the unborn appear as specks, grains of dust cut off from any before or after.
Where the city of the dead reassures the living, the city of the unborn gives no security, only alarm.

One possibility: the unborn vastly outnumber all the living and dead together, invisible crowds fill every pore of the stone, packed on the sides of the funnel like spectators in a stadium, and since each generation multiplies, every funnel opens into hundreds of further funnels, each holding millions of unborn who stretch their necks and open their mouths to keep from suffocating.

The other possibility: Laudomia will vanish one day and the generations will stop at a certain number; then the city of the dead and the city of the unborn are the two bulbs of an hourglass that is never turned over, each passage from birth to death a grain through the neck, and the last inhabitant to be born is the last grain, waiting now at the top of the heap.
visualConcept: Laudomia is built as a colossal hourglass floating in a pale haze, glass bulbs in a dark walnut and brass frame, with its three cities stacked along one vertical axis. At the narrow waist sits the living Laudomia: a compact walled city of tall crammed tenements, stacked balconies and tiny windows, with a round open well at the centre of its piazza through which a thread of light falls. The upper bulb is the house of the unborn, a vast and empty marble funnel of tiered niches, brackets, capitals and plinths rising like the stands of a stadium under a hollow coffered dome, every ledge dusted with tens of thousands of trembling motes of light, the unborn as small as ants' eggs, and at the very top of the rim one slightly larger grain that waits alone. The lower bulb is the city of the dead: a stepped heap of windowless tomb blocks faced with grids of name-slabs, cut by alleys just wide enough for a gravedigger's cart that repeat the street plan of the living city above, where small visitors stand reading names on a fine afternoon. A continuous trickle of glowing grains falls from the funnel's spout through the living city onto the heap of the dead, and with every grain that lands one more slab lights and settles into place. The image states the city's final thought directly: the dead and the unborn are the two bulbs, the living are the neck, and no one turns the glass.
layout: Frame: walnut discs with brass rims (radius 17, 0.8 thick) centred at y +24 and y -21.6, joined by four turned brass columns at radius 16.5 (azimuths 45, 135, 225, 315). Glass: a lathe envelope through the profile points (r, y) = (11, 23.5), (15, 18), (15.5, 12), (12, 5), (7.6, 0), (12, -5), (15.5, -12), (15.2, -19), (14.8, -21.2), nearly invisible except for Fresnel rim light. Living city at the waist: disc platform radius 7.4, top at y 0, 1.0 thick; crenellated circular wall (r 7.2, h 1.0) with four gates; about 70 tenements (2-5 storeys of 0.45, 0.7-1.2 wide) on 8 radial streets and 2 ring streets; central piazza r 1.4 with an open well (r 0.35) straight through the platform; about 260 inhabitants; two stairs spiral down from the north and south gates onto the heap. House of the unborn: an inverted marble cone from its spout (r 0.35 at y +3) to its rim (r 14 at y +18), 18 stadium-like tiers, each riser an arcade of empty arched niches with jutting brackets, little capitals and plinths (about 1,400 niches); a hollow ribbed and coffered shallow dome over the rim (y 18 to 23); 40,000 instanced points for the unborn, densest near the spout; faint aubergine veins in the marble along which tiny violet and bronze motes drift in procession (the future crowds in eggplant-coloured robes and turkey-feather turbans). The last grain: one point three times larger on the top tier. City of the dead: 12 stepped terraces from an apex (r 1.5, y -2.5) to a base (r 14, y -21.2), built of windowless blocks faced with about 2,600 small slabs, alleys 0.4 wide following the living city's radial-and-ring pattern scaled up; 20 visitors and one gravedigger's cart. Grain stream: about 6 grains per second along the central axis from y +3 down to the heap's apex.
signatureMotion: 1) The fall: a thin continuous thread of bright grains pours from the funnel's spout through the well in the piazza onto the apex of the heap; the motes of the unborn creep slowly down the tiers toward the spout, and each grain that lands lights one new slab, which slides down to a vacant place on the terraces, so the city of the dead visibly fills tier by tier while the funnel slowly drains. 2) A life in passing: every few seconds one grain stops in the piazza with a soft flash and becomes a tiny person, who walks a street, passes out through a gate and down the spiral stair to the terraces, where it dims back into a grain and is filed into a slab; meanwhile small groups of visitors pause before slabs that glow faintly as they read their own names. 3) Waiting: the unborn motes shiver and stretch upward in tiny flickers like necks craning for air, the violet processions crawl along the marble veins, and the last grain on the rim pulses once every four seconds.
interactionDescription: Switches between the two thoughts that trouble Laudomia's visitors. Off: the finite hourglass, glass and frame intact, the last grain waiting on the rim. On: the glass and frame dissolve; every niche of the funnel opens into a smaller funnel lined with its own tiers of shivering motes, and each of those opens further funnels (three levels of recursion, spreading outward and upward past the frame into the haze); the motes multiply into a galaxy of dust, the falling thread thickens, and the last grain vanishes because there is no longer a last one. Toggling back folds the funnels in and closes the glass round the city again.
mood: A fine, clear afternoon, the kind on which the living visit their dead. Low slanting gold light pours into the marble funnel and makes it glow like a sunlit stadium full of dust motes, while the heap of the dead lies in cool lavender shade; the glass catches long highlights; the air is still and pale. Serene on the surface, vertiginous underneath: a silence measured by falling grains.
caption: Laudomia is three cities, not one. Beyond its walls spreads the city of its dead, where every life has been filed into order and the living come on fine afternoons to read their own names. Elsewhere waits the city of the unborn, an empty hall of niches where the future crouches as fine as dust. The dead console; the unborn unsettle. Each life is a grain slipping through the narrow waist between them.
motto: Every life is one grain; no one turns the glass.
camera: Level with the waist from about 62 units, elevation 8 degrees, target (0, 1, 0), field of view 42, so the whole hourglass stands centred and upright with the living city at the optical centre and both the funnel's rim and the heap's base in frame. Continuous slow orbit at about 2 degrees per second; zoom range 18 (close enough to watch the piazza and the falling thread) to 80.
